911.title: the Nayanars
911.hook: two mangoes, one hungry guest, and a husband who wants the second one
911.howItsDone: Karaikkal Ammaiyar is honored among the Nayanars in Shiva temples, and in Karaikkal a mango festival remembers the story of the two mangoes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Nayanars, the Tamil saints of Shiva, and Kannappa, the hunter who worshiped all wrong and gave his own eye.

Two mangoes arrive at a merchant's house in the port town of Karaikkal. The merchant sent them home for his lunch. His wife, Punitavati, puts them aside. Then a knock: a wandering devotee of Shiva, worn out and hungry. She has rice but nothing to go with it, so she gives him rice and one of the mangoes. He eats, blesses her, and goes. Then her husband comes home, eats the remaining mango, loves it, and says: bring me the other one.
screen: `TWO MANGOES.` → `ONE GOES TO A HUNGRY GUEST.` → `BRING ME THE OTHER ONE.`

segments.voice: The Periya Puranam tells it like this. Punitavati goes into the kitchen and prays to Shiva, and a mango appears in her hand. She serves it. It's sweeter than the first, so sweet her husband asks where it came from. She tells him the truth. He doesn't quite believe her: then get me another, he says. She prays again, another mango appears, and the moment he takes it, it vanishes. Now he's afraid. Not angry: afraid. His wife is clearly more than he bargained for. So he quietly sails away on business, settles in another town, marries again, and names his daughter Punitavati. When her family finally finds him, he bows before her as if she were a goddess. Here's the turn. Punitavati doesn't ask for him back. The story says she asks Shiva to take away the beauty she kept for her husband and give her the form of a pey, a gaunt, skeletal, ghost-like being. And it happens. She sets out for Shiva's mountain, and when she reaches it, the Periya Puranam says, she goes up on her head, upside down, so her feet won't touch the holy ground. Shiva sees her coming and calls her Mother. From then on she's Karaikkal Ammaiyar, the mother of Karaikkal. She sings of Shiva dancing in the cremation ground, and asks only to stay at his feet, singing, while he dances. And it all grew from one mango, given to a stranger at the door without asking anyone.
screen: `A MANGO APPEARS IN HER HAND.` · `HE SAILS AWAY, AFRAID.` · `SHE ASKS TO LOSE HER BEAUTY.` · `SHIVA CALLS HER MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Picture your own front door, and someone knocking who needs something small. Notice what you'd have to give, and the voice that says save it, someone might ask later; don't argue with it, just breathe beside it. If you pray, pray for whoever may knock on your door this week, in words you already know.
The Nayanars. The Tamil saints of Shiva. Karaikkal Ammaiyar is the woman of the mangoes, whom Shiva called Mother.
Your line: the woman of the mangoes. Shiva saw her coming and called her Mother. Until tomorrow.

912.title: the Nayanars
912.hook: milk on a small boy's lips, and a father who wants to know who gave it
912.howItsDone: Tamil Shaivas sing hymns from the Tevaram in temple worship, often led by singers called oduvars, and the story of Sambandar and the milk is remembered at the Sirkazhi temple.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Nayanars again. Karaikkal Ammaiyar gave a mango to a stranger at her door, and Shiva called her Mother.

A father leaves his little boy on the steps of a temple tank and wades in to bathe, ducking under the water to say his prayers. On the steps, the boy can't see his father and starts to cry, calling for his mother and father, looking toward the temple tower. When the father comes up, the crying has stopped. The boy is calm. And there's milk on his lips. Nobody else is there.
screen: `A BOY ON THE TEMPLE STEPS.` → `HE CRIES FOR HIS PARENTS.` → `MILK ON HIS LIPS.`

segments.voice: The town is Sirkazhi, and the boy is known as Sambandar. In the Periya Puranam, when he cries, Shiva and Parvati come to the tank, and Parvati, the Mother of the world, feeds him milk from a golden cup. Then they're gone. His father, a careful Brahmin, sees the milk and is furious. Who fed you? Food from a stranger's hand could break the rules he lives by. He picks up a stick. And the small boy, instead of explaining, points up at the sky and sings. That song, as tradition remembers it, describes the one who wears an earring in his ear, who rides the bull, who wears the pale crescent moon, and then calls him the thief who stole my heart. It's a description of Shiva. The boy's answer to who fed you is: him. Sambandar keeps singing all his life, going from temple to temple, singing of each place. His songs, with those of two other Nayanars, Appar and Sundarar, are gathered as the Tevaram, and Tamil Shaivas still sing them in temple worship. Put our three Nayanars side by side. Kannappa offered with his hands. Karaikkal Ammaiyar offered at her door. Sambandar offers with his voice. And his father isn't a villain. He's a man of rules, and a little scared for his son, and the story answers him not with a lecture but with a song.
screen: `PARVATI'S CUP OF MILK.` · `WHO FED YOU?` · `HE POINTS UP AND SINGS.` · `THE TEVARAM: SONGS FROM TEMPLE TO TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: Think back to a time someone took care of you when you thought you were alone, fed you, found you, calmed you down, and stay with the moment the crying stopped. If someone asked who fed you, where would you point? If you pray, give thanks to God, or to whoever it was; if not, let the memory be enough.
The Nayanars. The Tamil saints of Shiva. Sambandar is the boy fed milk by Parvati, whose songs are sung in the Tevaram.
Your line: he points up and sings. Sometimes the best answer to an angry question is to point. That's day nine hundred twelve.

913.title: Jnaneshwar
913.hook: four children turned away, and a buffalo that recites the Veda
913.howItsDone: Jnaneshwar is honored across Maharashtra, especially by the Varkari tradition; his shrine is at Alandi, and stories of his childhood, including the buffalo at Paithan, are told and staged by devotees.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Nayanars one last time. Sambandar, milk on his lips, pointed at the sky and sang his answer to who fed you.

Four children walk into a town of learned Brahmins with a request. Three brothers and a little sister, shut out by their community their whole lives, through no fault of their own. They want to be accepted. The scholars look them over and start to laugh. One points at a buffalo plodding by, and makes a joke about names. Today the path moves north and west, into the Marathi-speaking country, and meets the second of those children: Jnaneshwar.
screen: `FOUR CHILDREN, SHUT OUT.` → `THE SCHOLARS LAUGH.` → `A BUFFALO WALKS BY.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as tradition tells it. The children's father had left home to become a sannyasi, a renunciant. His teacher then sent him back to his wife and household life. To their community, a monk who goes home has broken the order of things, and the family is cast out. Four children are born into that: Nivritti, Jnanadev, Sopan, and their sister Muktabai. Before long, the story says, they're on their own. So they go to the Brahmins of Paithan to ask for a letter of purification that would let them belong. The scholars aren't moved. Hearing the second boy's name, Jnanadev, which carries the Sanskrit word for knowledge, someone mocks him: names mean nothing; look, that buffalo has a name too. Jnaneshwar doesn't argue. The story says he answers that the same Self lives in the buffalo as in him, and places his hand on its head. And the buffalo begins to recite the Veda, the sacred text these men have spent their lives learning. Another telling adds that when someone whips the buffalo, the marks rise on the boy's back. The scholars fall silent, and some tellings say they then grant the letter. Notice what the boy doesn't do. He doesn't prove he deserves to belong. In the story, he shows that the line they drew, between people worth hearing and creatures that don't count, was never real. And the voice comes from the lowest place in the scene: an animal in the street.
screen: `A MONK WHO WENT HOME.` · `THE BRAHMINS OF PAITHAN.` · `THE SAME SELF IN THE BUFFALO.` · `THE VEDA FROM AN ANIMAL'S MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a creature you rarely think about, a pigeon on a ledge, a dog on your street, an insect on the window, and let it be there, breathing too, alive in its own way. Then add a person you tend to look past, and hold them both, with no conclusions. If you pray, hold them before God in words you already use.
Jnaneshwar. Also called Jnanadev. The Marathi poet-saint who, the story says, made a buffalo recite the Veda to answer the people who shut his family out.

914.title: Jnaneshwar
914.hook: the Gita, carried out of Sanskrit and into the language of the street
914.howItsDone: Varkari devotees read the Jnaneshwari aloud in groups, at home and in temples, and many read it along the way on the pilgrimage to Pandharpur.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jnaneshwar, the outcast boy at Paithan who put his hand on a buffalo's head, and the buffalo recited the Veda.

A temple in a small town by a river. A young man sits near a stone pillar and talks, verse by verse, through the Bhagavad Gita. Not in Sanskrit, the language of the priests, but in Marathi, the language of the farmers, the potters, the women at the well, the people sitting in front of him. Beside him, someone writes every word down. Those talks become a book that people in Maharashtra still read aloud together.
screen: `A TEMPLE BY A RIVER.` → `THE GITA, IN MARATHI.` → `SOMEONE WRITES IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: Tradition says this happened at Nevasa, and that the man writing was Sachchidananda, taking down Jnaneshwar's words as he spoke. The book is the Jnaneshwari, named after him, and it isn't a translation in the usual sense. It walks through the Gita verse by verse and opens each one up with pictures from ordinary life: a tortoise drawing in its limbs, a lamp burning where no wind reaches. Images the Gita gives in a line, he lingers over. Remember Paithan, where scholars laughed at outcast children. Now one of those children takes a teaching most people met in Sanskrit, a language few of his listeners had studied, and opens it in the everyday language, for anyone who can listen. In one passage he makes a promise about his Marathi: he'll make his words so sweet they'd win a wager against nectar. Not a modest claim. It's a bet that the language of the street can carry the deepest things. And then the humility. All through the book, Jnaneshwar hands the credit to his teacher, Nivritti, who is also his older brother. He speaks of himself as a child, and of everything good in the book as his teacher's grace. The boldest claim about language, and the smallest about himself, in the same book. People in the Varkari tradition read the Jnaneshwari in groups, and walk with it on pilgrimage.
screen: `SPOKEN AT NEVASA, WRITTEN DOWN.` · `THE GITA OPENED IN MARATHI.` · `SWEETER THAN NECTAR.` · `ALL CREDIT TO HIS BROTHER.`

segments.voice: Think of one teaching, from any source, that only made sense once someone put it in plain words, a parent, a teacher, a friend at a kitchen table, and bring back their voice, the exact way they said it. Let gratitude for them be what you hold. If you pray, thank God for them; if not, say their name to yourself, once.

915.title: Jnaneshwar
915.hook: a yogi rides in on a tiger, and the children ride out on a wall
915.carry: a wall only has to be willing
915.howItsDone: Marathi-speaking devotees often recite the Pasayadan at the close of worship or gatherings, and pilgrims visit Jnaneshwar's samadhi shrine at Alandi, where his palanquin sets out on the Varkari pilgrimage to Pandharpur.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jnaneshwar again. The Gita opened in Marathi, sweeter than nectar, with all the credit given to his brother.

Here comes a yogi, riding a tiger. In his hand, instead of a whip, a live snake. Behind him, a crowd of disciples. His name is Changdev, and tradition remembers him as a man of great yogic powers. He's heard about a young saint at Alandi, and he's coming to see him, the way a man with powers might arrive. At the other end of the road, Jnaneshwar, his brothers and his sister are sitting on a low wall in the sun. Someone runs up: he's coming.
screen: `A YOGI ON A TIGER.` → `A SNAKE FOR A WHIP.` → `CHILDREN ON A WALL.`

segments.voice: It starts with a letter that was never written. Before setting out, Changdev wanted to send word ahead, but couldn't decide how to address Jnaneshwar. As an equal? A teacher? A boy? So he sent a blank sheet. Muktabai, the sister, is said to have read it and remarked that all his years of practice had left him blank. Then the tiger, the snake, the crowd. Jnaneshwar doesn't climb down. The story says he asks the wall to move, and the wall carries the four children down the road to meet the yogi. Changdev, who had mastered a living tiger, sees children riding on stone, and the pride goes out of him. Tradition says he became a disciple, some tellings say of Muktabai herself. A tiger has to be tamed. A wall only has to be willing. That's the joke at the heart of the story, and it's on anyone who thinks arriving has to be impressive. Now hold that beside how Jnaneshwar ends his book. At the close of the Jnaneshwari he asks God for a gift, a pasayadan, and it isn't for himself. He asks that the crookedness of the wicked fall away, that they come to love doing good, and that all beings become friends to one another. Tradition says that later, at Alandi, still a young man, Jnaneshwar entered samadhi, a final meditation, and his shrine there is honored as the place where he still sits. A boy who once begged for a letter, and later received a blank one, ended by asking for the whole world's good.
screen: `A BLANK LETTER.` · `THE WALL THAT MOVES.` · `A TIGER TAMED, A WALL WILLING.` · `THE PASAYADAN: A GIFT FOR ALL.`

916.title: Namdev
916.hook: a boy sets a bowl of milk before the god, and waits for him to drink
916.howItsDone: Varkari devotees sing abhangs, including Namdev's, in kirtan with cymbals, and the temple of Vitthal at Pandharpur keeps a step at its entrance named for Namdev.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jnaneshwar for the last time. The yogi on the tiger, the children on the willing wall, and a book that ends by asking good for all beings.
screen: `JNANESHWAR.` · `A WALL ONLY HAS TO BE WILLING.`

segments.voice: A bowl of milk sits on the temple floor at Pandharpur, before the image of Vitthal, the dark god who stands on a brick with his hands on his hips. A small boy has carried it there. His father usually brings the offering, but he's away, so today the boy has been sent. He sets it down, folds his hands, and waits. The god doesn't move. The milk doesn't move. The boy keeps waiting. Nobody has told him that offerings are usually received unseen.
screen: `A BOWL OF MILK FOR VITTHAL.` → `A BOY SETS IT DOWN.` → `HE WAITS FOR THE GOD TO DRINK.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Namdev grew up in a family of tailors devoted to Vitthal, the form of Krishna worshiped at Pandharpur, whom his devotees call by tender names like Vithoba and, sometimes, mother. As the story goes, the boy waits, and still the god doesn't drink. So he pleads. He's done what his father does; why won't you take it? Is something wrong with me? Some tellings say he cries; some say he threatens to break his own head on the stone floor if Vitthal refuses. And Vitthal, the story says, reaches out of the image and drinks the milk. All of it. The boy goes home with an empty bowl, and nobody believes him. It's a funny story, and it knows it. But for Namdev, the god isn't an idea, and the offering isn't a gesture. If you bring a friend milk, the friend drinks it. He takes Vitthal at his word, the way a child takes anyone at their word, and the story rewards him instead of correcting him. Namdev grows up to be a singer. His songs, called abhangs, are short devotional poems in which he talks to Vitthal like someone in the same room: pleading, teasing, complaining, longing. In the Varkari tradition, people still sing abhangs, Namdev's among them, in kirtan, call and response, with cymbals keeping the beat. Jnaneshwar gave the people the Gita in their own language. Namdev gives them something smaller and just as bold: permission to treat God like someone who might actually drink the milk.

917.title: Namdev
917.howItsDone: The stories of Gora the potter and Visoba Khechar belong to the Varkari tradition of Maharashtra, whose members sing the songs of Namdev and the other saints of Pandharpur in praise of Vitthal.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Namdev, the boy who set a bowl of milk before Vitthal and waited until, the story says, the god drank it.

A potter walks down a row of seated saints, holding the flat wooden paddle he uses on pots. He taps a pot and listens: fired all the way through, or still soft inside? The story says Jnaneshwar asked him, Gora the potter, to test the devotees gathered there. So Gora taps each head. Each saint sits quietly and takes it. Then he reaches Namdev, and Namdev bristles, and says so. Gora listens, and tells the whole room: this pot is still half-baked.
screen: `GORA THE POTTER.` → `HE TAPS EACH HEAD.` → `THIS POT IS HALF-BAKED.`

segments.voice: That stung, because Namdev's love for Vitthal was real. This is the boy whose milk, the story says, Vitthal drank, and who grew up talking to him like a friend. So he runs to Vitthal to complain. And Vitthal, in the story, takes the potter's side. You have love, he says. What you don't have yet is a teacher. Go and find Visoba Khechar. Namdev finds the old man in a Shiva temple, lying down, apparently asleep, with his feet resting on the linga, the stone that stands for Shiva. Shocked, Namdev wakes him. Visoba answers mildly. I'm old and tired. Lift my feet, please, and set them down somewhere God is not. Namdev moves them. A linga rises up under them. He moves them again. Another. Wherever the feet come down, Shiva is already there. At last Namdev sets them in his own lap, and he understands: there is nowhere to put the feet, because there is nowhere without God. So what was wrong with the pot? Not too little devotion. Devotion with walls around it, so fond of God in one image, in one town, that it couldn't hear him anywhere else. The potter heard the hollow place. The teacher didn't argue; he handed Namdev a puzzle he could only solve with his hands. Look back at this week. Sambandar pointed at the sky. Jnaneshwar touched a buffalo's head and asked a wall to move. And Namdev learned, from a man who seemed to break every rule, that the holy was already under his hands.
screen: `A POTTER CALLS HIM HALF-BAKED.` · `VITTHAL SAYS: FIND A TEACHER.` · `FEET ON THE LINGA.` · then, large: `NOWHERE TO PUT THE FEET.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ordinary place you'll be later: a bus seat, a sink full of dishes, a waiting room. Set your attention down there gently, the way Namdev set down those tired feet, and ask: what if this place isn't empty of what I call holy? If you pray, you can hold that place before God.
Namdev. The poet-saint of Pandharpur, called half-baked by a potter, who learned from Visoba Khechar that there's nowhere to put the feet where God is not.
